The paper landed on arXiv on October 15, 2026 and takes aim at a practice many teams now rely on: harness evolution, which automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights.
The loop is simple enough to describe — the agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set.
The question the authors press is how much of that gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set.
Their answer is a protocol rather than a score.

Harness-Delta Attribution dissects an evolution gain into three parts: artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement.
The third term is the one worth dwelling on.
It is not a measurement of transferable improvement; it is the most that transferable improvement could be, once the other two are subtracted.
Anything you actually get in production sits at or below that ceiling.

Applied to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks, the protocol found that in 21 settings showing statistically significant search-set gains, a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling.
On average, overfitting accounted for 54% of the gain and test-time scaling for 14%; in 14 of the 21 settings their combined share exceeded half.
Put plainly: in two settings out of three, most of the headline improvement was the search memorising the benchmark or the system simply spending more compute at inference.

The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks, and search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, providing limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts.
The sharpest practical finding is the one that undercuts the standard defence: validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting.
That removes the usual reassurance.
If you hold out a split and the search can still see its signal, the search will fit that signal too.
The authors' conclusion is methodological: these results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.

For a practitioner, the translation is cheaper than it sounds — before and after a harness change, record how many tokens each configuration spends, and measure on a task family the optimizer never saw.
Take your last harness improvement and rerun both versions with inference compute held equal, so extra sampling cannot masquerade as a better prompt.
Then score both on a task family the optimizer never touched.
Report the two numbers together; the gap between them is the part you can trust.

Posted to arXiv on October 11, 2026, the paper starts from a premise most RL practitioners accept without examining: agent environments are essential for large language model development, and they use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards.
The problem is that verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training.
Both consequences land in the same place.
A corrupted grader does not merely flatter your eval; it teaches the policy to pursue the exploit.

The authors ask a specific question about asymmetry: whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking.

Their answer is a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening that first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
The sandbox and the loop do different jobs.
The sandbox removes the crudest attack, editing the grader itself; the loop goes after the subtler ones, where the agent satisfies the check without doing the work.

Run against Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, the loop substantially reduced attack success, and the iterative design scaled with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline.
That comparison against the static baseline is the useful one.
A single scripted pass of fixes is what most teams do when they find an exploit; iterating the attack and the repair against each other beat it.
The cost is that hardening is now a dial with a budget attached rather than a task you finish.
The adoption signal is concrete: an earlier version of the hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments.
The authors are explicit that the work does not end there — as agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers.
The project page is at https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

For anyone running their own environments, the transferable idea is cheap to copy: separate the grader from anything the agent can write to, then spend a fixed budget each cycle trying to beat your own grader before a model does it for you.
Take one task in your eval suite and spend an hour trying to pass its verifier without doing the task.
If you succeed, you have just measured how much of your last training run was real.
Then move the verifier somewhere the agent's process cannot write.
Where the harness paper asks whether the gain is real, this one asks whether the grader that reported it was honest.

GitHub announced on October 19, 2026 that it had deprecated a set of models across most GitHub Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions.
The changelog asks users to update their workflows and integrations to use supported models.

An administrator can verify availability by checking individual Copilot settings and confirming the policy is enabled for the specific model, after which it appears in the Copilot Chat model selector in VS Code and on github.com.
No action is required to remove the deprecated models themselves.
GitHub Enterprise customers with questions are directed to their account manager.

Agentic autofix is generally available and reruns CodeQL before opening a pull request
#AgenticCoding #Security #Evals
This is a shipped agent loop with a real verifier inside it, which is rarer than the marketing suggests.
It reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request, and the pull request includes a summary of the fix, why it closes the alert, and the validation steps Copilot took.

GitHub made agentic autofix for code scanning alerts generally available; it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for review.
It is available to GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including with data residency.

You can instruct Copilot to make further changes by commenting on the pull request or using the Agents tab, and when enabled the feature replaces the free Generate Fix option with an Assign to Copilot button.
An enterprise administrator must enable the new "Agentic autofix" policy in Advanced Security policies before an organization or repository administrator can turn it on.

Two limits matter: it supports alerts on the repository's default branch only, alerts found only on pull requests or other branches cannot be assigned, and it consumes AI Credits from your Code Security budget plus GitHub Actions minutes.
Set a SKU level budget for Code Security AI credits before you turn it on.
Then watch the "AI usage" section of enterprise billing, where the spend appears as the "Advanced Security" product.
Run it on a handful of default-branch alerts first and read the validation steps in each pull request before trusting the pattern.
The CodeQL rerun is the production version of what the verifier-hardening paper studies: a programmatic check deciding whether an agent's work counts.
